title: How would you design a real-time COLLABORATIVE DOCUMENT editor like Google Docs: the core problem is merging CONCURRENT edits from many users without conflicts, so you need either Operational Transformation (OT: transform each incoming op against concurrent ops so all replicas converge, typically via a central server that orders operations) or CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types: structures that merge commutatively so replicas converge WITHOUT a central coordinator): plus persisting the op log / document snapshots, WebSockets for low-latency bidirectional sync, presence/cursors, offline edit buffering + replay on reconnect, and the trade-off between OT (simpler data, needs a server to order ops) and CRDTs (coordination-free, better for offline/P2P, but larger metadata)?
shortTitle: How would you design a real-time collaborative document editor like Google Docs (OT vs CRDT)
keyPoints: The core problem is merging concurrent edits so all replicas converge to the same final document (strong eventual consistency).
OT transforms operations against each other with a central ordering server; simpler data but complex transform logic.
CRDTs use stable unique character IDs instead of fragile positions, merging commutatively without a coordinator.
OT is simpler data and well-suited for server-coordinated editing; CRDTs are better for offline and P2P.
Persist an ordered operation log plus periodic snapshots for recovery, undo, and version history.
WebSockets provide low-latency bidirectional sync; edits are applied optimistically on the client.
Offline edits are buffered and replayed on reconnect; CRDTs handle this cleanly since ops commute.

s1_definition.oneliner: The hard problem is merging concurrent edits so all replicas converge; OT transforms ops with a central server, CRDTs merge coordination-free, both backed by an op log, WebSocket sync, and offline replay.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Convergence** – All replicas must reach the same document state despite edits arriving in different orders.
- **OT** – Transforms each operation against concurrent ones so applying them in different orders yields the same result; needs a central server.
- **CRDT** – Every character has a unique ID, not a position, so operations commute and merge without coordination.
- **Op log** – The ordered log of operations is the authoritative history; periodic snapshots accelerate recovery.
- **Offline** – Edits are buffered on the client; on reconnect, OT transforms them against missed ops, CRDTs simply merge.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh and Priya at National Bank of India both edit the same loan agreement. Rajesh inserts a word at the start while Priya deletes a word in the middle. If applied naively, positions clash and the document garbles. OT is a clerk who adjusts Priya's position to account for Rajesh's insert. CRDTs give every character a permanent ID so insertions and deletions never clash regardless of order.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core problem in a collaborative editor is merging concurrent edits from many users so every replica converges to the same document. At National Bank of India, Rajesh and Priya co-edit a loan agreement, and if Rajesh inserts at the start while Priya deletes in the middle, naive position-based application garbles the document. OT transforms operations against each other with a central server that assigns order, while CRDTs give every character a unique ID so operations commute without coordination.

OT has simpler, smaller data but needs a central server and famously tricky transform logic. CRDTs are coordination-free and handle offline editing cleanly since ops commute, but carry heavier per-character metadata and tombstone overhead. Modern libraries like Yjs and Automerge favor CRDTs. Around either engine, Pankaj persists an ordered operation log as the authoritative history with periodic snapshots for fast recovery.

Live sync uses WebSockets: the client applies edits optimistically for a snappy feel, sends over the socket, the server merges, and broadcasts. Presence and cursors are ephemeral signals on the same socket. Offline edits are buffered and replayed on reconnect, where CRDTs merge cleanly and OT requires transforming against everything missed.

Remember one sentence: Merge concurrent edits with OT (transform against each other via a central server) or CRDTs (commutative structures that converge coordination-free), backed by a persisted op log, WebSocket optimistic sync, and offline buffering with replay.
